title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training

Title:Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

report.summary: Navalia pairs verifiable synthetic task generation from corporate filings with long-horizon SFT and RL to build stronger Cowork Agents, beating its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base on five benchmarks.
report.background: LLM agents are shifting from chat assistants to "Cowork Agents" that plan, call tools and execute multi-step work. Financial analysis is a harsh test: agents must pull evidence from multiple documents and chain numerical reasoning without arithmetic or citation errors. The bottleneck is data. Expert-written tasks are slow and expensive, while naive LLM synthesis produces tasks that are too easy, have ambiguous answers, or leak the solution. Navalia attacks this by generating tasks whose answers are mechanically checkable: evidence is selected from complete fact sets and computation chains are executable, so every step has real data dependencies. Independent LLM review plus programmatic checks filter bad samples before they enter training. The verified tasks then feed trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, a recipe increasingly common for turning general models into reliable long-horizon workers.
key_points: Verifiable synthesis is the core idea: tasks are built by picking supporting evidence from a complete set of facts and wiring an executable computation chain, so intermediate steps depend on real data rather than being invented by the model. Each task therefore ships with traceable evidence and a checkable ground-truth answer.

Two-layer verification filters the data: an independent LLM reviews evidence consistency while programmatic checks confirm the final numeric answer. This combination catches the two common failure modes of synthetic data, ungrounded evidence and wrong answers, before noisy samples reach the training pipeline.

Training is a three-stage pipeline: verified tasks generate solution trajectories, which drive cold-start supervised fine-tuning, followed by reinforcement learning to sharpen long-horizon execution. SFT teaches the format and tool habits; RL optimizes the multi-step behaviour.

Results generalize beyond finance: starting from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Navalia improves on all five benchmarks (OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, Workspace-Bench-Lite), with gains on general office tasks suggesting the method transfers outside the financial domain.

The paper argues the real constraint on agent progress is high-quality, hard, verifiable task data, not model scale alone, and offers a repeatable synthesis recipe that others can apply to new domains.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Navalia reinforces a shift: progress on agents increasingly comes from data engineering and post-training pipelines rather than bigger base models. Verifiable synthesis with programmatic answer checks gives labs a scalable alternative to expert annotation, and the finance-to-office transfer suggests domain recipes are reusable. For developers, the practical lesson is that SFT warm-up plus RL on filtered trajectories is now a standard playbook, and that building cheap verifiers for your own domain is the highest-leverage investment. For regular users, expect agents that cite where numbers came from and show their work on multi-step tasks, with fewer silent arithmetic errors. Caveat: results come from a single 35B-scale model and five benchmarks, so independent replication is still needed.
report.tools: Follow the benchmarks to evaluate your own agents: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA and Workspace-Bench-Lite. For implementation, watch Qwen3 MoE models as a base, OpenHands and LangGraph for agent scaffolding, verl or TRL for RL post-training, and the Hugging Face ecosystem for checkpoints and datasets. SEC EDGAR filings are a practical source if you want to rebuild a small verifiable financial task set yourself.
